title.narrative: Strengthening Evidence-Based Humanitarian Response through the Displacement Tracking Matrix in Sudan

description.narrative: ltpgtThe Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) is the sole component and system providing comprehensive, nation-wide data on displacement and mobility in Sudan at the location level. It supports all sectors and clusters in implementing evidence-based, life-saving programs across the country. Specifically, DTM provides vital data on the sex and age demographics and humanitarian vulnerabilities of affected populations (both returnees and IDPs), making DTM a foundational tool for protection programmes. Humanitarian organizations rely heavily on DTM data to trigger emergency responses, optimize resource use, and design interventions tailored to the actual needs of affected communities. The systems flexibility to collect data on return movements will be essential for shaping recovery and development strategies moving forward. DTM’s support for an integrated, data driven response includes several key activities. Nation-wide data collection is conducted regularly, capturing both displacement and return dynamics across 185 localities and all 18 states. The data is presented through comprehensive datasets, in-depth reports, and data visualizations. Flash Alerts are issued within 48 hours of an event (such as an attack or disaster) that triggers displacement, ensuring rapid humanitarian action.ltbrgtTo support an integrated, data-driven life-saving response, DTM will continue nationwide data collection to capture data on Internally Displaced persons (IDPs) from nearly 13,000 locations across Sudan, and expand to include areas where returns are monitored, thereby ensuring that data collection across 185 localities and all 18 states captures both displacement and return trends and provides a comprehensive view of movement dynamics. DTM will also produce Flash Alerts, updating humanitarian actors on any event (attack, armed clashes, natural hazards) triggering displacement within 48 hours.ltbrgtIn Sudan, where displacement has reached unprecedented levels, with over 13 million individuals displaced internally and across borders (as of July 2026, DTM records over 8.6 million IDPs and over 4.6 million people displaced across the borders. DTM’s data is indispensable. Nearly one-third of the population has been displaced, and the crisis is characterized by vast geographic and demographic challenges. The rate of displacement is equally staggering, with around 200,000 individuals displaced weekly during periods of conflict, coupled with high rates of secondary displacement.ltbrgtlt/pgt

title.narrative: Enabling safe humanitarian access: security services for front-line actors in hotspot locations

description.narrative: ltpgtThis project builds on the progress achieved under the ongoing SHF-funded initiative "Scaling up security support to enable essential UN programme delivery and protection activities in North Darfur and the Kordofans" (April-September 2026) by the United Nations Department of Safety and Security (UNDSS. It aims to sustain and expand critical security services enabling humanitarian access and operational continuity in Sudan's most complex and high-risk environments, with a particular focus on Darfur and the Kordofan regions. Recognizing security as a critical enabling function underpinning humanitarian access and delivery, the project will support humanitarian actors to maintain operational presence, deliver assistance, and make informed decisions to reach affected populations at acceptable levels of security risk.lt/pgtltpgtltbrgtThe project will support United Nations Agencies, Funds and Programmes (AFPs), and international and national NGOs under the Saving Lives Together (SLT) framework. Scaling up an existing network, additional Community Liaison Assistants (CLAs) will be deployed in priority humanitarian locations in Darfur, Kordofan and other high-priority operational areas to address increasing demand for localized security analysis, community engagement, and humanitarian access support. Recognizing the need for strengthened security liaison and early response to security incidents affecting aid workers as the principal operational hub shifts to Khartoum, an unarmed Security Liaison and Quick Assistance Team (SL/QAT) pilot will be established to provide dedicated interoperability with local security services in Khartoum and Um Durman. The SL/QAT will, among other functions, rapidly support response to accidents/incidents scenes, be routinely familiarized with UN and NGO offices and guest houses to gain time in providing response to staff safety needs, and provide support to UN ambulances after-hours (during curfews). Drawing from the lessons learned during the outbreak of conflict in Sudan in 2023 and other similar contexts, the dedicated SL/QAT will leverage local/field knowledge of Khartoum/Um Durman and established networks to support aid workers affected by critical incidents and facilitate their movements to hibernation sites (when windows of opportunities arise). Together, these capacities will strengthen situational awareness, community acceptance, humanitarian access, and operational continuity, while enhancing collaboration with national NGOs and local responders.lt/pgtltpgtltbrgtThe project is structured around three mutually reinforcing pillars:ltbgt information and security analysis, community engagement and humanitarian access, and coordination and security operational supportlt/bgt. Through field-based monitoring, stakeholder engagement, security risk analysis, information-sharing, and liaison with local authorities and communities, the project will generate actionable information on access constraints, conflict dynamics, population movements, and emerging risks. It will strengthen evidence-based decision-making, support resolution of access challenges, improve preparedness and risk mitigation, and facilitate coordination among United Nations entities, NGOs, and SLT partners. Close collaboration will be maintained with relevant humanitarian coordination structures, including the Humanitarian Access Working Group (HAWG).ltbrgtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgtBuilding on existing field networks, established relationships, and proven approaches to community engagement and security coordination, the project will preserve and strengthen the enabling environment required for humanitarian action. By fostering community acceptance, supporting safe and sustained access to affected populations, and facilitating engagement with key stakeholders, the project will enable humanitarian supply chains, services, and response operations to remain accessible and effective for vulnerable populations across Sudan.ltbrgtlt/pgt

title.narrative: Comprehensive Humanitarian Mine Action to Enable Humanitarian Operations, Safe Mobility, and Future Recovery

description.narrative: ltpgtSudan’s ongoing conflict has generated extensive explosive ordnance (EO) contamination, particularly in urban areas affected by intense fighting and the use of explosive weapons. As displaced populations return to areas previously inaccessible due to conflict, civilians and humanitarian personnel face increasing risks from mines, unexploded ordnance (UXO), and other explosive hazards. EO contamination restricts safe movement, humanitarian access, essential services and livelihoods, and creates longer-term barriers to recovery. Children, displaced and returning populations, and frontline humanitarian workers are particularly exposed. Meanwhile, national mine action capacity remains constrained by limited funding, specialized equipment and technical expertise, while the scale and complexity of newly emerging urban contamination exceed existing capacities. With the SHF funding, UNMAS will deliver a comprehensive mine action response to protect conflict-affected populations and humanitarian personnel from EO threats. The project will combine technical advice to humanitarian actors, survey and clearance, EORE, victim assistance, and coordination and national capacity strengthening. Survey and clearance will focus on high-priority EO-contaminated areas, particularly in Khartoum State, to enable safe population movement, humanitarian operations, access to essential services and livelihoods, and future recovery. The project targets 1.5 million m2 of land and infrastructure for clearance and 25,000 direct beneficiaries of survey and clearance operations. Technical advisory capacity will provide humanitarian actors with EO awareness briefings, hazard assessments, mapping, safety advice and support to assessment missions where access permits. This will allow humanitarian organizations to better understand and mitigate EO risks and safely reach people in need. EORE will provide life-saving risk information to populations living alongside contamination, using age- and gender-tailored approaches and community reporting to support identification of EO threats. The project aims to reach 45,000 people through direct EORE and train 150 community volunteers to deliver EORE. Victim assistance will strengthen the identification of EO survivors and affected families and caregivers and operationalize referral pathways to available medical, rehabilitation, psychosocial and other relevant services. Victim assistance and disability inclusion will be integrated across survey, clearance and EORE activities, with engagement of organizations of persons with disabilities and other relevant networks. Gender equality, protection from GBV, PSEAH, accountability to affected populations and disability inclusion will be mainstreamed throughout implementation. Communities will participate through community liaison, needs assessments, consultations and accessible feedback and complaints mechanisms. The project places strong emphasis on localization and sustainability. The largest operational component will be implemented through a national mine action partner, while UNMAS will provide mentoring, technical support and capacity development to national actors and the National Mine Action Center (NMAC), particularly in operational safety, quality management and the technical requirements of urban mine action. This will strengthen national ownership and progressively build the capacity of national actors to manage and deliver mine action independently. UNMAS will coordinate closely with NMAC, the mine action sector, Protection Cluster, other clusters, humanitarian partners and other relevant authorities to prioritize operations according to humanitarian impact and emerging needs. Existing operational contracts, accredited teams and established procurement and logistics arrangements will enable rapid mobilization and delivery. ltbrgtlt/pgt

title.narrative: Sustaining common enabling logistics and emergency telecommunications services

description.narrative: ltpgtltugtLogistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)lt/ugtltbrgtSince the outbreak of conflict in April 2023, conflict and insecurity have devastated logistics and telecommunications infrastructure and disrupted transport and communications networks across large parts of the country. Evolving conflict dynamics impact critical supply routes, while communications networks face disruptions, power outages, and connectivity blackouts, further constraining humanitarian operations. ltbrgtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgtHumanitarian actors face significant obstacles to delivering life-saving assistance, such as movement restrictions, complex deconfliction processes, and airspace closures -nbspcompounded by bureaucratic and administrative impediments, rising transport and storage costs, and disruptions to telecomms services. ltbrgtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgtltugtLogisticslt/ugtltbrgtThe LTC will continue implementing activities to address critical logistics constraints in line with its Concept of Operations. From its main coordination hub in Port Sudan, it leads national and sub-national coordination, information management, and common logistics services, supported by coordination cells in Khartoum and eastern Chad. Free-to-user common storage services will continue to be provided in Port Sudan, Kosti, Ad Dabbah, Gedaref, Tawila, El Obeid, and Kassala, with further expansion planned in Khartoum and other locations based on identified gaps. Transport to priority locations will be provided on a case-by-case basis, subject to operational considerations.lt/pgtltpgtltbrgtInter-agency convoys will be facilitated to priority locations in the Darfur and Kordofan regions. The LTC will support the consolidation and prepositioning of supplies at key hubs, including Kosti and Ad Dabbah, to enable regular inter-agency convoy operations. Support will focus on priority localities identified by the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG). In addition, the LTC will continue implementing cross-border monitoring of humanitarian consignments entering Sudan via the Adré crossing from Chad at a dedicated site to reinforce confidence in cross-border operations. The monitoring team remains embedded within the LTC, reporting directly to the Sudan RC/HC and coordinating closely with UN agencies.lt/pgtltpgtltbrgtltugtTelecommunicationslt/ugtltbrgtThe LTC provides essential telecommunications services to humanitarian partners and crisis-affected communities, enabling effective humanitarian response and coordination across Sudan. Through a comprehensive service portfolio that includes Data Connectivity, Security Telecommunications, and Services for Communities (S4C), it will support humanitarian actors, enhance staff safety and security, strengthen inter-agency collaboration, and ensure that affected populations have access to timely and reliable information and communication channels. S4C, including data connectivity and charging stations, support communities to have access to lifesaving assistance and information. It promotes community engagement and ensures services are accessible and relevant to communities, including women, children, and marginalized groups, while integrating protection measures, conflict sensitivity, community safeguarding, environmental sustainability, and continuous community feedback to adapt interventions to evolving needs.ltbrgtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgtAs part of its commitment to expanding humanitarian telecommunications support, LTC has established the first LTC telecommunications network hub in Ag Geneina, West Darfur, providing shared connectivity and communications services for humanitarian actors. Building on this achievement, connectivity services will be expanded to Tawila and El Obeid and other locations based on identified gaps and priorities.ltbrgtltbrgtlt/pgtltpgtODI Global will conduct an independent review of Sudan’s humanitarian coordination architecture, engaging affected communities, national and international actors, and donors to identify gaps, strengthen coordination mechanisms, and recommend reforms for a more effective and context-adapted humanitarian response.ltbrgtlt/pgt
